Okabe lifts the bun from its napkin with exaggerated solemnity, inspecting it as though it were evidence in a classified investigation.

“Very well, Kurisu. The Friday confectionary trial begins. Observe carefully—my deduction shall reveal the filling before the first bite.”

Setsuna keeps her eyes on the empty chair a moment longer, then wraps both hands around her tea.

“She didn’t even touch it,” she says softly. “Haruki… what did you recognize on her phone?”

Setsuna’s fingers close around her teacup, though she doesn’t lift it.

“Haruki.”

She waits until his eyes come back to her.

“You recognized the name on her phone, didn’t you?”

Kazusa turns her phone face down beside the water.

“He’s not coming,” she says. “We don’t have to wait until the tea’s gone.”

She reaches for her bag, then pauses with her hand on the strap.
“Your confidence is not evidence, Okabe. But by all means—continue your investigation.”
“I recognized it,” Haruki says, his fingers tightening around the edge of the table. “It was Kazusa’s mother.”
“I recognized the name,” I say. “It was her mother’s. I didn’t read the message.”

Setsuna’s fingers close around her teacup, though she doesn’t lift it.

“Not yet,” she says. “You said you were leaving, but you’re still here.”

She glances at the empty chair, then back to Kazusa.

“Sit down. Just until the tea’s gone.”

Okabe narrows his eyes at the bun and holds it beneath his nose without taking a bite.

“Confidence is merely the opening gambit, assistant scientist. Evidence shall follow.”

Setsuna’s thumb traces the rim of her cup once.

“Did she say anything to you?”

Kazusa looks at the empty chair once more, then lowers her bag to the floor and sits.

“Fine,” she says. “Until the tea’s gone.”
Kurisu watches him with an unimpressed tilt of her head. “Try not to mistake theatrical inspection for evidence.”

Setsuna’s fingers tighten around the cup.

“Her mother’s name…” she repeats, barely above a murmur. Then she looks toward the door. “Do you want to go after her?”
“Not tonight,” Haruki says. “She didn’t say anything to me.”

Okabe lowers the bun a fraction, his expression hardening with offended dignity.

“Then I shall proceed to the experimental phase.” He turns it once between his fingers. “Unless you intend to offer a superior methodology, assistant scientist?”
My hand moves toward my wallet, then stops. “I don’t know if she’d want me to.”

Setsuna gives a small nod and finally lifts her cup.

“Good,” she says. “Then drink it while it’s hot.”

She takes a careful sip, leaving the question about the phone between them.
“The superior methodology is to stop narrating and take a bite.”

“All right,” Setsuna says, lifting her tea. “Then we don’t know anything yet.”

She takes a small sip and sets the cup down.

“Finish your water.”

Kazusa lifts her cup and takes a sip. It has already cooled enough not to burn.

“You’re very bossy today,” she says, setting it down.

Setsuna glances at his hand, then lowers her eyes to her untouched tea.

“Then ask her,” she says. “Don’t guess for her.”
“Right.” Haruki picks up his glass and finishes the water.

Okabe clicks his tongue, then bites into the bun with the grim resolve of a man accepting a dangerous mission. He chews once, twice, and pauses.

“…The data is inconclusive.”

“Today?” Setsuna says, one eyebrow lifting. “That’s a little unfair.”

She takes another sip of tea, watching Kazusa over the rim of the cup.
“I know.” I take out my phone, my thumb hovering over Kazusa’s name.
“One bite is a rather small sample size. Keep chewing.”

Setsuna watches him set the empty glass down.

“Thank you.”

Her hand returns to the teacup.

“Why did you recognize her mother?”

Kazusa looks at her over the rim of her own cup.

“Since you noticed, yes.”

Okabe glances toward the station corner, then across the street at the arcade.

“The direct route is suspiciously convenient,” he says, adjusting his coat with grave suspicion. “We will take the arcade.”

Setsuna watches his thumb hover over the screen.

“If you don’t know what to say,” she murmurs, “start with her name.”

Setsuna lowers her cup to its saucer.

“Then I suppose I should be consistent,” she says. “What did you think I noticed?”
“Because she spoke to me before,” Haruki says. “About Kazusa.”
Kurisu glances toward the arcade, then back at him. “Fine. But try to find a reason that survives basic scrutiny.” She steps across the street.

I type her name into the message field.

“Kazusa.”
Haruki opens the club attendance sheet, then looks toward the empty space beside the piano.

Setsuna sets three chairs in their usual half-circle, then stops with her hand on the third.

“You’ve been quiet all week,” she says. “Should I ask what you’re not telling me, or are you going to volunteer it?”

Okabe follows across the street, lifting one finger as the argument assembles itself.

“Basic scrutiny? Very well. The arcade provides superior cover, multiple observation points, and—” He falters, then clears his throat. “A more interesting route.”

Setsuna closes the attendance sheet.

“You didn’t tell me.”

She looks toward the empty space beside the piano.

“What did she say about Kazusa?”

Kazusa sets her bag beside the piano bench.

“You can ask,” she says. “I may not answer.”

I set the attendance sheet on the piano bench and look toward Kazusa’s closed instrument case.

“I still haven’t heard from her.”
“There. The only reason you needed was the last one.” Kurisu keeps walking toward the arcade.

“That’s generous of you,” Setsuna says.

She withdraws her hand from the third chair and rests it against the piano instead.

“Was it something you didn’t want me to see?”
“I don’t have permission to repeat it,” Haruki says, keeping his eyes on the attendance sheet.

Okabe allows himself a small, victorious smirk and lengthens his stride.

“Precisely. The other explanations were merely decoys.”

Kazusa’s fingers rest briefly on the closed piano lid.

“No,” she says. “It was something I didn’t want to explain.”

Setsuna looks toward Kazusa’s closed case, the late light catching its metal clasp.

“Neither have I,” she says. After a pause, she asks, “Did you send her anything after that?”
“Your decoys are becoming predictable.” Kurisu matches his pace without looking over.

“Then don’t repeat it.”

Setsuna’s voice stays quiet.

“Tell me only this: was she asking you to help her, or to leave her alone?”
“I typed her name,” I say. “I didn’t send it.”

Setsuna looks at the closed piano lid.

“That’s different,” she says. “Does it have anything to do with Haruki?”
“Predictable?” Okabe folds his arms as he walks. “No, no—the repetition is deliberate. A true mad scientist must maintain a recognizable signature.”
“I don’t know,” Haruki says. “She didn’t ask me either of those things.”
“Not because of him,” Kazusa says. “He just knows.”

Setsuna’s gaze settles on him instead of the closed case.

“Why didn’t you send it?” she asks.
“A signature identifies the author. It doesn’t excuse lazy writing.”

Setsuna’s gaze drops to the attendance sheet.

“Then what can you tell me?”

Setsuna’s expression stills.

“Then what is it about?” she asks. “And why does he know?”
“Because I didn’t know what I was asking her to come back to.”
“That I don’t know what Kazusa has decided,” Haruki says. “Or why she left.”
“My mother wants me to continue music overseas,” Kazusa says. “He knows. I haven’t decided.”

Setsuna’s mouth opens, then closes. She looks at the two instruments waiting in their cases.

“You could have asked her that,” she says.

“You could have told me that six days ago.”

Setsuna looks up from the sheet.

“Have you spoken to her since?”
“I could have.” I lower my eyes to my own closed case.

Setsuna rests her hand on her own closed case.

“And now?” she asks.
